newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium may use gold-sale FX for debt - Verplaetse.
newsitem.headline: Belgium may use gold-sale FX for debt - Verplaetse.

text.p: Central bank governor Alfons Verplaetse said on Friday Belgium might use foreign exchange reserves generated by previous gold sales to help cut its national debt.
Gold sales in the past five years have left the central bank with 236 billion francs in the form of foreign exchange reserves on its books, on which the government receives interest.

"I do not exclude that in order to make our balance sheet more transparent...it might be that a part of this capital gain should be used, without influencing the deficit, to reduce the gross debt," Verplaetse told Reuters Financial Television.
"This is not window dressing, it is a real transaction. We will reduce our public debt in foreign currencies for that amount," he said.
Verplaetse said the Belgian government aimed to cut its debt to gross domestic product ratio by 10 percent between 1993-97.
Belgium's debt, the highest in the European Union, was 137.9 percent of GDP in 1993 and is forecast to fall to 131.8 percent of GDP by the end of 1996.
"(The reduction) will be done firstly by reducing the budget deficit, by selling some public assets and by better management of the public debt," Verplaetse said.
Belgium's 1997 budget, currently being negotiated by ministers, is due to be presented to parliament on October 1.

At present the Belgian National Bank's statutes prevent its gold being used directly to help cut the debt, although a small fraction, around 2.75 percent, can be used to mint and sell commemorative coins, the proceeds from which go directly to the Treasury.
Since the law on the gold reserves was drawn up in 1987 a little over two percent of the gold has been used in this way.

"We have important gold assets. In the last years we have sold some and the capital gain we got is a liability of the central bank the counterparty of which is foreign currencies on which the government receives interest," Verplaetse told RFTV.

Under the Maastricht Treaty rules for economic and monetary union (EMU), countries joining a single current must have brought their debts to 60 percent of GDP or be approaching that level at a "satisfactory pace."

Belgium's net debt, which forms the greater part of the gross debt as defined for the purposes of Maastricht, was 9,828 billion Belgian francs in August, of which roughly 970 billion was held in foreign currencies.
Verplaetse said that although the debt was high, it was more than compensated by the country's high national savings rate.
Belgium already meets other criteria in the Treaty on inflation, long-term interest rates and exchange rate stability.
The government has said its main objective is to make sure Belgium fully qualifies by reducing its public deficit to below the EMU target of three percent of GDP by the end of 1997.
The deficit is forecast by the central bank to be around 3.1 percent of GDP at the end of 1996.
Including the 236 billion franc capital gain on recent gold sales, the National Bank's foreign exchange reserves amounted to 408 billion francs on September 16.
In addition the bank held the equivalent of 173 billion Belgian francs in gold bullion.
